claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially stabilized in a high-temperature BCC state.
The range of phases formed during cooling is driven by feedback between local compositional fluctuations and kinetic limitations.
Longer residence in the 1250–1350 °C range affects phase nucleation.
Slower cooling or an isothermal hold in the 1250–1350 °C range permits local atomic diffusion and reordering.
Limited atomic diffusion produces or amplifies local concentration variations.
Local compositional heterogeneities at grain boundaries or within grains act as preferential nucleation sites for secondary phases.
The heterogeneous regions lower the kinetic barrier to nucleation.
Slower cooling promotes formation of a metastable FCC phase in addition to the BCC matrix.
Rapid quenching suppresses the secondary-phase transformation by suppressing diffusion.
Rapid quenching preserves a predominantly BCC structure with minimal local compositional variation.
Slower cooling or isothermal holding will increase the non-BCC phase fraction relative to rapid quenching.
The proposed behavior applies only when atomic mobility is sufficient for local reordering but insufficient for complete equilibration.
Extreme rapid cooling lies outside the applicable regime because diffusion is effectively suppressed.
Very slow cooling or extended high-temperature annealing lies outside the applicable regime because equilibrium thermodynamics may dominate phase selection.
Thermal gradients, diffusion rates, and local composition jointly affect the magnitude and spatial distribution of secondary phases.
A lack of a statistically significant secondary-phase increase or a lack of measurable segregation in the slow-cooled samples would falsify the hypothesis.
